newsitem.title: USA: Wis. governor proposes $36.5 bln, two-year budget.
newsitem.headline: Wis. governor proposes $36.5 bln, two-year budget.

text.p: Wisconsin Gov. Tommy Thompson on Wednesday proposed a $36.5 billion, fiscal 1998-99 all-funds budget that is aimed at maintaining the state's committment to fund two-thirds of the cost of primary and elementary schools.

Under the Republican governor's plan, schools would see a $204.3 million increase in state general and catagorical aids in fiscal 1998 and another $194.2 million increase the following fiscal year. State aid to schools would total nearly $3.8 billion in fiscal 1999.
The legislature enacted the higher state funding scheme a few years ago as a way to lower local property taxes.

Thompson called for the creation of a state-wide public school choice program beginning in fiscal 1999. Last month, the Dane County Circuit Court found a school choice program that included church-based private schools to be unconstitutional.
The state's general purpose revenue budget would be $9.5 billion in fiscal 1998 and $9.8 billion in fiscal 1999, under Thompson's proposal.
Thompson's budget projects state revenues would grow by 4.6 percent or nearly $400 million in fiscal 1998, which begins July 1, and by 4.8 percent or $434 million in fiscal 1999.
The budget calls for the issuance of about $500 million of operating notes in fiscal 1998 and another $750 million in fiscal 1999.

Other bond proposals included $50 million in general obligation bond issuance as part of the governor's proposed five-year, $500 million Technology for Educational Achievement plan. Proceeds from the bond sales would be loaned to schools to upgrade electrical and network wiring to accomodate computers, according to budget materials.

On Monday, Thompson proposed a $200 million enviromental program that included $15.5 million of GO bonds for landfills and $22 million of GO bonds to match an estimated $110 million in federal grants for a new safe drinking water revolving loan fund.

The governor recommended using $35 million in federal highway fund to lower the amout of debt financing for major highway projects in fiscal 1998 and to reduce interest costs. Budget documents indicated the move would reduce the share of such projects' development costs supported by bonding to 47 percent in fiscal 1998 from 68 percent in the current fiscal year.

A December report by the Legislative Audit Bureau had warned that debt service payments on bonds sold for major highway projects will exceed the amount of proceeds from future debt issuance by the turn of the century.

Thompson also called for a $7.5 million increase in the Wisconsin Housing and Economic Development Authority's bond authorization to expand the Beginning Farmer Bond Program to $17.5 million from $10 million.

The governor budgeted $335.6 million over the bienium for his massive overhaul of welfare, called Wisconsin Works. He proposed using federal grant funds to complete a state takeover of child welfare services in Milwaukee County set for Jan. 1.

As for Medicaid, Thompson proposed general fund spending of $924.3 million in fiscal 1998 and $943.9 million in fiscal 1999. The budget included increases for both nursing homes and inpatient hospitals.

Thompson proposed a new lottery credit that would be paid to all property tax payers based on total levies starting in December. The state's current lottery credit system was ruled unconstitutional by the Dane County Circuit Court because it excluded vacation homeowners.
